picks.title: Nirvana is NOT Nothing | There IS an Unborn, Uncreated, Unconditioned | Nibbana | Ajahn Dhammasiha
picks.summary: The final goal of Dhamma practice, what it's all about, is to realize Nibbāna (Sanskrit: Nirvāṇa ). It's important to have an accurate understanding of our final objective, otherwise it would be difficult to develop our mind in the right direction. However, as Nibbana / Nirvana is totally beyond all concepts, words, notions and thoughts, even the Buddha can not possibly describe it accurately by means of language. He can only provide similies to inspire us, or he describes what Nibbāna in NOT. For example, the Buddha has stated many times that Nibbana is the end of birth, ageing and death; Nib
picks.reason: Clear explanation of Nirvana as the ultimate Buddhist goal beyond concepts.

picks.title: Sitting Like a Buddha
picks.summary: Where are you located in your body? Most of us, without ever having chosen it, sense ourselves somewhere behind the eyes. Zazen instructions typically bundle two separable practices: disidentifying from thinking, and relocating the self in the belly. Contemporary mindfulness often teaches the first and omits the second. Zen's own instruction is to sit as a buddha rather than in order to become one, trusting a monastic container to do that work silently; outside such a container, this talk suggests, it has to be made explicit. picks.reason: Zen talk on bodily awareness and sitting as a Buddha, not just becoming one.

picks.showTitle: Sounds True: Insights at the Edge
picks.title: [ENCORE EPISODE] Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche: "In Love with the World"
picks.summary: At 36, Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche walked out of his monastery in the middle of the night with a few thousand rupees and no plan. Weeks later, he was dying of food poisoning on a street in India—and chose not to call for help. In this encore episode, Tami Simon speaks with the beloved Tibetan Buddhist teacher about what he found on the other side of that night.Rinpoche is now partnering with Sounds True on a brand-new course, Wild World, Steady Mind: 21 Days to Embrace Modern Reality with Clarity and Calm, filmed on location at his monastery in Nepal. Visit soundstrue.com to learn more.See Privacy
picks.reason: Tibetan Buddhist teacher shares insights from a life-changing experience.

picks.title: This One Note Is Enough | Chodo Robert Campbell
picks.summary: “We don't have to save everyone, solve everything, or understand the whole mystery of our lives. All we have to do is be in this moment, this breath, this body. Then bow, let go, and listen.”Chodo Sensei shares the story of Kakua, one of the first Japanese monks to travel to China and study Zen. A recluse who preferred remote mountains to monastery fame, Kakua was eventually summoned by the emperor to demonstrate the true teachings he'd acquired. picks.title: The First Precept Is Not a Rule - It's a Practice of Freedom
picks.summary:
In this talk, Jessica Gibbons explores the first Buddhist precept through the lens of intention, harm, and our responsibility to all living beings. She explains how non-harming is not a rigid moral rule, but a living practice of mindfulness, discernment, and compassion that helps us reduce suffering in daily life.
1 of 5 in a series. 
This talk was given by Jessica Gibbons at Wild Heart Meditation Center in Nashville, TN. 
Support Wild Heart Meditation Center here: https://www.wildheartmeditationcenter.org/donate
Enjoy!
